strengths: Addresses an underexplored and relevant problem: cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning with irregular continuous-time interactions.

The combination of an HJB/PINN critic, model learning, TD anchoring, and value-gradient supervision is coherent and potentially useful; the controlled oscillator provides interpretable value and gradient comparisons against an analytical solution.
Experiments cover continuous-time adaptations of MPE and several multi-agent MuJoCo tasks, use multiple seeds, and report broadly favorable learning curves.
Ablations examine VGI, individual critic losses, activation functions, and loss weighting, providing some evidence that value-gradient supervision is practically important.
weaknesses: The theoretical formulation is internally inconsistent. Equation (2) defines an infinite-horizon, time-independent value without a terminal cost, whereas the subsequent HJB analysis uses a finite-horizon, time-dependent value with boundary condition V(x,T)=g(x). The treatment of discounting and the terminal cost in the appendix is also inconsistent.

The VGI derivation is not mathematically sound as written. Equation (11) uses the Jacobian of the continuous-time vector field where differentiating the transition requires I+Delta-t times that Jacobian; the appendix later inserts this missing term, while the implementation instead differentiates a learned next-state model. These define different updates. Dependence of actions on state is also omitted without establishing conditions under which an envelope argument applies.

Theorem 3.4 is false under its stated assumptions. A bounded dynamics Jacobian does not imply contraction: the claimed factor exp(-rho Delta-t)(1+L_f Delta-t) is below one only under an additional relation such as rho>L_f locally. Taking Delta-t small merely makes the factor approach one and can leave it above one.

Lemma 3.3 claims pointwise policy improvement after a sufficiently small actor gradient step, but its proof assumes an exact greedy policy update. A stochastic gradient step with function approximation and sampled advantages does not provide the stated guarantee.

The empirical comparison does not adequately test the central claim against discrete-time MARL. Modern baselines such as MAPPO or MADDPG, equipped with the time interval as input and trained under the same variable-step protocol, are absent from the main MPE and MuJoCo experiments; MADDPG appears only in a toy time-step plot. The adaptation and tuning of the primarily single-agent continuous-time baselines are insufficiently documented.

The evidence is difficult to audit quantitatively: there are no numerical result tables, confidence intervals or significance tests, and some visual claims are stronger than the plotted agreement. Computational cost and sample efficiency are not reported despite the added dynamics model, reward model, automatic derivatives, and multiple critic losses.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details—including loss weights, the MPE time-step range, baseline architectures and hyperparameters, update frequencies, evaluation protocol, and code availability—are missing. The claimed decentralized execution is also unclear because the formal actor is conditioned on the global state, while the appendix later lists local observations as policy inputs.

strengths: Addresses the relevant and underexplored problem of cooperative multi-agent control with irregular decision intervals.
The combination of an HJB/PINN critic, learned dynamics and reward models, TD anchoring, and value-gradient consistency is intuitively motivated.
Experiments cover a controlled oscillator, two MPE tasks, and six Multi-Agent MuJoCo tasks, with several useful ablations.
weaknesses: The central convergence result is incorrect as stated. The proof yields a contraction factor exp(-rho*dt)(1+L_f*dt), which is not necessarily below one merely because the Jacobian is bounded and dt is small; approximately, an additional condition such as rho>L_f is needed. The theorem statement and proof also use inconsistent mappings.

The VGI derivation is inconsistent about whether f denotes a continuous-time vector field or a next-state transition. Equation 11 omits the identity and time-step factors required for the Jacobian of an Euler transition. It also does not justify ignoring the dependence of the policy action on the state.
Lemma 3.3 is unsupported: one gradient step on the proposed policy loss does not guarantee pointwise policy improvement. Its proof assumes the expected-Q improvement that it is supposed to establish.

The formulation mixes finite- and infinite-horizon objectives. Equation 2 integrates to infinity and omits the terminal cost, whereas the surrounding formulation and HJB use a finite horizon and terminal boundary condition. Notation for V(x) versus V(x,t) and the interpretation of rho are also inconsistent.

The empirical evidence is insufficiently auditable. Results are primarily plots, without numerical summaries, confidence intervals, significance tests, or quantitative value/gradient errors. Baseline tuning and compute parity are not documented.

The environments remain discretized simulations with random Euler steps or frame skips. The comparison does not adequately rule out strong discrete-time agents conditioned on the elapsed time, so improvements cannot be attributed cleanly to the continuous-time formulation.

Reproducibility is weak: important interval ranges, loss weights, optimization settings, update schedules, baseline hyperparameters, and evaluation details are missing. The claimed five-seed protocol also conflicts with the table listing seeds 111–120.
The CTDE claim is unclear because the derivation conditions decentralized policies on the global state, while the architecture table instead specifies local observations.

Inconsistent VIP/VPI naming, questionable LQR sign conventions, and several overbroad claims further reduce confidence. Because the invalid theoretical guarantees concern the paper's central contributions, the work is not competitive in its current form.

strengths: Addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: reinforcement learning for cooperative multi-agent systems with continuous, irregular decision times.
The combination of an HJB/PINN critic, a learned dynamics model, and value-gradient consistency is intuitive and potentially useful.
Evaluation spans a controlled oscillator with analytical ground truth, two MPE tasks, and six multi-agent MuJoCo tasks; the reported learning curves show substantial and generally consistent gains.
Ablations examine VGI, individual critic losses, activation functions, loss weighting, and robustness to changing time intervals.
weaknesses: The central VGI convergence theorem is incorrect under its stated assumptions. Bounded dynamics Jacobians do not imply contraction: e^{-rho*dt}(1+L_f*dt)<1 generally requires a condition such as rho>L_f, and taking dt small does not establish it.

The policy-improvement lemma does not prove the stated result. Its proof assumes exact greedy maximization of Q, whereas the implemented method takes a stochastic gradient step on -A log pi; a sufficiently small gradient step does not guarantee pointwise Q improvement.

The formulation is internally inconsistent: Eq. 2 defines an infinite-horizon, time-independent value without a terminal cost, while the subsequent HJB uses a finite horizon, time-dependent value and terminal boundary condition. The VGI equations also alternate between the Jacobian of continuous dynamics and that of a discrete transition model.

The experimental comparison is insufficient for a top-tier MARL claim. Standard strong MARL baselines such as MAPPO, MADDPG, and FACMAC are largely absent from the main benchmarks; MADDPG appears only in the simple oscillator test. It is therefore unclear whether the gains come from continuous-time modeling or comparisons against weak/adapted baselines.

The paper provides curves but no numerical result table, confidence intervals or hypothesis tests. It says the main results use five seeds, while the hyperparameter appendix lists seeds 111–120, creating an unresolved reproducibility discrepancy.

Important implementation and fairness details are missing, including the actual MPE time-step range, critic loss weights, baseline tuning and architectures, evaluation protocol, and computational-cost comparison. No code or environment release is identified.

The method still learns discrete next-state dynamics and recovers derivatives through finite differences, so the claimed avoidance of discretization is overstated; sensitivity to model error and very small or out-of-distribution time intervals is not adequately studied.

strengths: Addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: scalable reinforcement learning for irregularly sampled, continuous-time cooperative multi-agent systems.
The proposed combination of an HJB/PINN critic, TD-style anchoring, learned dynamics and reward models, and explicit value-gradient supervision is intuitively motivated.

The empirical study spans a didactic control problem, MPE, and several multi-agent MuJoCo tasks, with five seeds, uncertainty bands, component ablations, activation/loss-weight studies, and some noise and timestep sensitivity analysis. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/ddd6f3dadd1642d59bafbe20fdc17681/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central convergence theorem is incorrect as stated. Boundedness of the dynamics Jacobian does not imply contraction: the paper's bound is beta=exp(-rho*dt)(1+Lf*dt), which for small dt behaves as 1+(Lf-rho)dt and can exceed one whenever Lf>rho. Making dt smaller alone therefore does not establish beta<1. Moreover, autonomous/time-invariant dynamics do not imply that their Jacobian is constant along a trajectory, contrary to the proof, and gradients at different states are treated as iterations of one fixed affine map.

The VGI equations are internally inconsistent. For a continuous-time vector field, differentiating x_{t+dt}=x_t+f(x_t,u_t)dt requires the transition Jacobian I+dt*J_f, which is absent from the main estimator but appears later in the appendix. The implementation instead learns a next-state predictor and uses its Jacobian, while the HJB residual requires the continuous-time vector field. These distinct objects are denoted by the same f, leaving the actual algorithm and claimed theory mismatched.

Lemma 3.3 does not establish its claim. It asserts pointwise Q improvement after one sufficiently small gradient step on the stochastic actor loss, but its proof silently replaces that update with exact greedy maximization of Q. A policy-gradient step generally provides neither the stated pointwise guarantee nor the chain of inequalities used in the proof, especially with an approximate critic.

The purported analytical ground truth in the coupled-oscillator experiment is problematic. Since the paper maximizes a negative quadratic reward, the return/value should be non-positive, yet it defines and plots V*=x^T P x as positive. The reported CARE also omits the continuous discount rate, uses an unconstrained LQR solution despite bounded actions, and the displayed dynamics contain no cross-agent coupling despite being called a coupled spring-damper system. These issues undermine the main controlled validation of value and gradient accuracy.

The critic residual is called an optimal HJB residual but is evaluated at sampled actions from the current policy rather than maximizing the Hamiltonian. This corresponds more closely to policy evaluation; the manuscript does not rigorously connect the resulting alternating approximate updates to the optimal HJB equation.

The experimental comparisons do not establish fairness under irregular timing. VIP's policy explicitly receives the time interval, while it is unclear whether discrete-time baselines receive the same information or use elapsed-time-aware discounting and reward-rate scaling. Holding a per-step discount fixed under variable frame skips creates exactly the bias attributed to those baselines. Adaptation and tuning of the continuous-time baselines are also insufficiently documented.

The benchmarks remain numerically discretized systems with randomly varied Euler steps or MuJoCo frame skips. The paper does not disentangle benefits of continuous-time reasoning from benefits of conditioning on dt, model learning, extra critic losses, or unequal baseline adaptation.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the advertised code link is missing, important quantities such as lambda_anchor and lambda_g, MPE timestep ranges, optimizer/update schedules, baseline hyperparameters, and precise reward/time normalization are absent. Results are mostly curves without numerical summaries or statistical tests. Because the main theoretical guarantees are false and key empirical evidence is confounded, the central claims are not currently supported.

strengths: The paper targets an important and relatively underexplored problem: cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning with continuous-time dynamics and irregular decision intervals.

Combining an HJB/PINN critic with explicit value-gradient consistency is intuitively motivated, and the paper evaluates the idea on an analytical oscillator example plus continuous-time adaptations of MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo.
The experiments include several useful diagnostic studies, including removal of VGI, loss-component ablations, activation-function comparisons, timestep sensitivity, and robustness to dynamics noise.
weaknesses: The central VGI convergence theorem is incorrect under its stated assumptions. Boundedness of the dynamics Jacobian does not imply exp(-rho*dt)(1+Lf*dt)<1; for small dt this requires approximately rho>Lf. Moreover, time-invariant nonlinear dynamics do not have a state-independent Jacobian. Thus the claimed contraction and unique fixed point are unsupported.

The VGI definition and implementation are mathematically inconsistent. Differentiating a transition x_next=x+f(x,u)dt produces the Jacobian I+dt*df/dx, whereas Eq. 10 uses df/dx directly. The paper later redefines the learned dynamics model as a next-state predictor, while the HJB requires a continuous-time vector field. Dependence of actions on state is also omitted without a valid envelope-theorem argument.

The policy-improvement lemma does not establish its stated result. Its proof assumes an exact greedy policy-improvement operation, while the algorithm takes one stochastic gradient step using an approximate learned advantage. Such a step does not guarantee pointwise Q^{pi_new}(x,u)>=Q^{pi_old}(x,u), particularly with function approximation and simultaneous multi-agent updates.

The analytical oscillator evaluation has a serious sign and discount inconsistency. The framework maximizes a negative running reward, so the optimal return should be negative, but the reported LQR value is the positive cost x^T P x. The CARE used for the purported ground truth also omits the discount-rate term required by the discounted objective. This undermines the main ground-truth validation.

The experimental protocol is insufficiently specified for fair reproduction. The MPE timestep range is omitted; adaptations and hyperparameters of the continuous- and discrete-time baselines are not adequately documented; reward integration and timestep-dependent discounting are unclear; and the promised code link is absent.

The evidence is largely qualitative learning curves. There are no tables of final means, standard deviations, confidence intervals, statistical tests, model errors, or computational costs. Shaded regions are not defined, the text reports five seeds while the appendix lists seeds 111-120, and discrete-time comparisons cover only a subset of tasks.

There are important formulation contradictions: policies condition on the global state in the method but on local observations plus the timestep in the appendix, making the decentralized-execution claim unclear. The HJB residual is evaluated at actor actions rather than maximizing the Hamiltonian, so it is not generally the optimal HJB equation claimed in the text.

Given the invalid theoretical guarantees, questionable analytical ground truth, and incomplete evaluation details, the central claims are not sufficiently supported for a top-tier venue; substantial theoretical and empirical revision would be required.

strengths: Addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: reinforcement learning for cooperative multi-agent systems with continuous and irregular decision intervals.
The combination of an HJB/PINN critic, a learned dynamics model, and explicit value-gradient supervision is intuitively motivated and potentially useful.
The empirical scope is broad, covering a controlled oscillator, two MPE tasks, and six multi-agent MuJoCo tasks with several continuous-time, discrete-time, and ablated baselines.
The paper includes useful diagnostic experiments on VGI, critic losses, activation functions, time intervals, and stochastic perturbations.
weaknesses: The central VGI derivation is mathematically inconsistent. For continuous dynamics, differentiating the next state requires the transition Jacobian I+Δt∇f, whereas Eq. 10 uses ∇f directly. The paper later treats fψ as a next-state predictor, conflating the continuous vector field with the discrete transition map.

Theorem 3.4 is false under its stated assumptions. A bounded dynamics Jacobian does not imply contraction: e^{-ρΔt}(1+LfΔt)<1 generally requires a condition such as ρ>Lf, and taking Δt small does not establish it. Moreover, time-invariant nonlinear dynamics do not have a state-independent Jacobian, contrary to the proof.

Lemma 3.3 does not justify the implemented actor update. Its proof replaces a single policy-gradient step with an exact greedy maximization of Q, and standard policy-improvement results do not imply the claimed pointwise inequality Q^{πnew}(x,u)≥Q^{πold}(x,u) for every state-action pair.

The oscillator validation appears sign-inconsistent: the method maximizes a negative quadratic reward, so the optimal value should be -x^T P x with gradient -2Px, but the appendix uses positive x^T P x and 2Px. This undermines the main ground-truth validation of value and gradient accuracy.

The experimental evidence is difficult to audit: results are primarily learning curves without numerical final-performance tables, uncertainty summaries, significance tests, or quantitative value/gradient errors. Seed reporting is also inconsistent between the stated five seeds and the 111–120 range in the hyperparameter table.

The continuous-time claim is overstated because the environments and learned dynamics remain explicitly discretized. It is unclear whether rewards are consistently converted into rates, whether all baselines receive the sampled time interval, and whether comparisons control for physical simulation time rather than episodes.

The CTDE/decentralized-execution formulation is ambiguous: the equations condition every agent policy on the global state, while the architecture table refers to observations. Baseline adaptations to multi-agent and irregular-time settings are insufficiently specified.

Reproducibility is below the expected standard: the abstract says code is available at a link, but no actual link is present, and important implementation details such as loss weights, time-interval ranges for MPE, baseline tuning, and precise gradient-target construction are missing.
